name: Mesoamerican religion
areas: San Lorenzo and La Venta on the Gulf Coast
the Zapotecs of Monte Albán, later the Mixtecs
from the first cities to the Itza kingdom of Petén
the shaft tombs, later the Tarascan kingdom
day-keepers and old rites within Catholic practice
routes: The Feathered Serpent honoured from Tula to Chichén Itzá
marks: The Olmec centre of San Lorenzo, with the earliest monumental religious art of Mesoamerica (around 1200 BCE).
The Olmec ceremonial centre of La Venta, with its great earthen pyramid (around 900–400 BCE).
The Zapotec capital, founded around 500 BCE on a levelled mountain top.
The Pyramid of the Sun was completed around 200; the Aztecs later believed the sun was born here.
Stela 29 (292) is the earliest known dated monument of the Maya lowlands.
A great Maya city of northern Yucatán, with its sacred cenote.
The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in 1325, by tradition where Huitzilopochtli had promised; its Great Temple was rededicated in 1487.
The friar Diego de Landa burned Maya books and images here in 1562.
The Spanish took Nojpetén, capital of the Itza, the last independent Maya kingdom, in 1697.
notes: The Olmecs of the Gulf Coast build the first great ceremonial centres, with colossal heads and images of their gods.
La Venta becomes the main Olmec centre, and Olmec symbols spread through Mesoamerica.
The Zapotecs found Monte Albán; carvings there and in the Maya lowlands record the 260-day ritual calendar.
In the Maya lowlands, El Mirador and other cities raise huge pyramids for the gods and the ancestors of their rulers.
Teotihuacan grows into the largest city of the Americas; the Pyramid of the Sun is completed around 200.
The Maya of the lowlands raise dated stelae (Tikal, 292) and honour divine kings who offer their own blood to the gods.
Classic Maya kingdoms such as Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copán build temples to their gods and ancestors; Teotihuacan declines.
The southern Maya cities are abandoned; Chichén Itzá and Tula honour the Feathered Serpent.
The Mexica found Tenochtitlan (1325), where by tradition their god Huitzilopochtli had promised.
The Aztec Empire rededicates the Great Temple of Tenochtitlan with the sacrifice of many captives (1487).
The fall of Tenochtitlan (1521) ends the Aztec state religion; friars destroy temples and books (Landa at Maní, 1562), while old rites survive in secret.
The Spanish take Nojpetén (1697), the last independent Maya kingdom; Maya day-keepers still count the 260-day calendar today.
src: Mary Miller and Karl Taube, The Gods and Symbols of Ancient Mexico and the Maya (1993)
